先生:xian1sheng5.note: Reordered for a learner. The generated order led with "teacher", which is a comparatively rare/regional sense of 先生 in modern Mandarin; the overwhelmingly common HSK-1 usage is the polite address term "Mr./sir" (X先生) and "husband". Leading with "teacher" risks confusion since 老师 (already HSK-1) is the standard word for teacher. No senses added or removed, only reordered — check 3 (glosses ordered sensibly for a learner).

日:ri4.note: Dropped the trailing "(vulgar) to fuck; to have sex with" sense. It is accurate CC-CEDICT content, but 日 (sun/day/date) is one of the very first characters an absolute beginner learns, and surfacing an unrelated vulgar slang sense unprompted on that card serves no HSK-1 pedagogical purpose and is inappropriate for a beginner-facing flashcard with no content warning or context. This is a per-card call, not a blanket policy on vulgar CC-CEDICT senses generally — see LR-002 Escalations for the broader policy question raised to the project owner.

星期:xing1qi1.note: Added a qualifier to the bare "Sunday" sense CC-CEDICT lists. This is genuine, correct content (星期 alone can colloquially mean Sunday, paralleling 礼拜), but presented as a bare, unqualified sense it risks a beginner concluding 星期 generally means "Sunday" rather than "week" — check 3 (not misleading out of context).

senses: which? (colloquial pronunciation of 哪, used before a classifier or numeral-classifier)
哪:nei3.note: Added a parenthetical connecting this card to 哪:na3, the other HSK-1 card for the same headword. The bare CC-CEDICT gloss ("which? (interrogative, followed by classifier or numeral-classifier)") doesn't explain the relationship, and without it a beginner seeing two separate 哪 cards with near-identical meaning but different readings could reasonably conclude they are unrelated words rather than a genuine, common colloquial pronunciation variant (as in 哪个, něige) of the same word already taught as 哪:na3. Kept as an approved, separate card (not flagged) because něi is a real, frequently-heard pronunciation, not a source-list artifact.
